title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
summary: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns—just to name a few examples.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked trusted source written by researcher(s) proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Pixabay/CC0 Public Domain The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns—just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters that tallies costs weeks after an event. NOAA stopped updating it in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting , which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events—a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts . The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars . This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five "billion-dollar" disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year—a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. As weather damage worsens, critical data is missing. One reason is NOAA's decision to retire its "Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters" database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact—and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity . Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. In 2025, the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government's preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline , while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites .
